To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the correctness statements of most verification efforts are not as general as the statements of the most general efforts, and that the correctness statements used by most efforts are not as precise as the statements of any effort.

the correctness statement of the most widely used approach to superscalar microprocessor verification (the approach of the Stanford Microprocessor Verification Group) is a special case of the correctness statement that we propose for use with the state-machine-based approach to superscalar verification, and that the state-machine-based correctness statement that we proposed is a special case (with a very narrow parameter space) of the correctness statement of a classical approach to microprocessor verification.
the correctness statement for a superscalar processor can be characterized as a set of safety properties, and the safety properties are parameterized by the processor width.
In summary, our research is concerned with
developing a common language for discussing microprocessor verification, and in particular with identifying the relationships between correctness statements.
the following questions: What is the nature of the correctness statements used in the verification of superscalar microprocessor implementations and specifications?
understanding the relationships between the different correctness statements and with providing a common framework for classifying and comparing different approaches.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the correctness of a superscalar microprocessor can be established by verifying the correctness of the state machine with the following properties: 1) the state machine is a deterministic finite state machine; 2) the state machine has a finite number of states; 3) the state machine can be implemented in a finite number of gates; 4) the state machine implements the instruction-set architecture; 5) the state machine satisfies the safety property.
the processor correctly executes all instructions in the order that the instruction-set architecture specifies.

the processor is correct with respect to the instruction-set architecture, and the correctness statement is based on the processor's state machine, the processor's control unit, and the processor's datapath.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the different approaches are complementary and that a combination of them is needed in order to verify a superscalar microprocessor correctly.
the correctness statements in the literature can be classified into a framework that is independent of implementation representation and verification technique.
the correctness statement for the safety of superscalar microprocessor designs is a statement of equivalence between the instruction-set architecture specification and an instruction-level model.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in order to compare and contrast the different approaches, it is necessary to first establish a common framework for classifying the correctness statements.
the correctness statements of most existing verification efforts are not as strong as those of the best known efforts.
there are many different ways to specify the safety properties of a microprocessor, and the different approaches are not necessarily incompatible.
